findings.issue_text: packages/types/Calendar.d.ts:134 — [P1, confidence 100] `destinationCalendar?: DestinationCalendar[] | null;` silently changes the webhook-facing CalendarEvent contract from an object/null to an array/null without versioning, so existing webhook consumers that read `payload.destinationCalendar.externalId` break on every newly emitted booking payload.

packages/features/bookings/lib/handleNewBooking.ts:1874 — [P1, confidence 100] `destinationCalendar: evt.destinationCalendar && evt.destinationCalendar.length > 0 ? { connect: { id: evt.destinationCalendar[0].id } } : undefined` persists only the first element of the new multi-host destination model, so later cancellation, reminder, reschedule, and webhook flows reload a one-element array and lose every secondary host destination; the strongest rebuttal is that booking references retain calendar IDs, but those references do not reconstruct the destinationCalendar payload consumed by those flows, so the model remains lossy.

packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:251 — [P1, confidence 100] `: event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId;` removes the former fallback to the event's destination calendar when a legacy booking reference has no `externalCalendarId`, so updates for those existing bookings send an undefined `calendarId` and no longer reach the calendar that originally held the event.

packages/core/EventManager.ts:339 — [P2, confidence 75] `for (const destination of event.destinationCalendar) {` serializes one credential lookup and one remote calendar creation per collective host, making booking latency and request-timeout risk grow linearly with host count; the strongest rebuttal is that collectives are usually small, but no bound is enforced, and batching credential IDs plus parallelizing independent creates deletes the per-host query/await structure without changing behavior.

packages/features/bookings/lib/handleNewBooking.ts:992 — P1 confidence 75: `if (isTeamEventType && eventType.schedulingType === "COLLECTIVE" && user.destinationCalendar)` omits every collective co-host without an explicit destination-calendar row, so those hosts receive no calendar event instead of the existing primary-calendar fallback; the strongest counterargument is that only configured destinations are in scope, but a collective booking promises every selected host an event and this branch silently excludes an otherwise valid host.

docs/tasks/task-001.md:2 — P2 confidence 100: `Review the change.` supplies no acceptance criteria or verification matrix for collective multi-host creation, update, cancellation, reschedule, mixed integrations, or missing destination calendars, so the task can be declared done while required lifecycle paths remain unverified; the strongest counterargument is that the title conveys intent, but it does not define observable success or edge-case behavior.

packages/core/EventManager.ts:119 — P1, confidence 100: `if (evt.location === MeetLocationType && mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration !== "google_calendar")` fails TypeScript compilation under strict null checks because destructuring `evt.destinationCalendar ?? []` gives `mainHostDestinationCalendar` the type `DestinationCalendar | undefined` and the code dereferences it without a guard.

packages/core/EventManager.ts:119 — [P1, confidence 100] `if (evt.location === MeetLocationType && mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration !== "google_calendar")` dereferences `undefined` when a Google Meet booking has no destination calendar, crashing the booking instead of executing the intended Cal Video fallback.

packages/core/EventManager.ts:369 — [P1, confidence 100] `if (credential) { const createdEvent = await createEvent(credential, event, destination.externalId); ... }` silently emits no result when a collective host's referenced credential is missing, so the booking passes the `results.length > 0` failure checks and reports success while dropping that host's calendar event; although skipping a deleted credential avoids aborting other hosts, the absence of an error result makes the partial failure invisible and therefore remains defective.

packages/core/EventManager.ts:597 — [P2, confidence 100] `return Promise.resolve(calendarReference?.map((reference) => { ... success: false ... }))` swallows every exception from multi-calendar updates after constructing but never logging `message`, leaving operators without the exception or affected credential needed to diagnose user-visible stale calendar events; although callers receive failure flags, those generic flags cannot identify the failure and the removed log makes the path unobservable.

packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:165 — [P2, confidence 75] `calendar.events.patch({ ... calendarId: selectedCalendar, ... });` fires the description patch without awaiting or handling its callback and passes `undefined` after an insert falls back to `"primary"`, so Google Meet creation resolves successfully while the hangout-link description update fails invisibly; although the event itself exists, recipients receive stale meeting details and no retry or error reports the failed second operation.

packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:254 — [P2, confidence 100] `const selectedCalendar = externalCalendarId ? externalCalendarId : event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId;` always resolves `undefined` on the fallback branch because it searches for an undefined external ID, causing updates of legacy references without `externalCalendarId` to fail instead of using the destination calendar; although new references carry the ID, existing bookings created before that field was populated still hit this runtime path.

goldens.comment: A null reference occurs in GoogleCalendarService.createEvent() and updateEvent() when mainHostDestinationCalendar is destructured from evt.destinationCalendar but evt.destinationCalendar is null or an empty array, causing mainHostDestinationCalendar to be undefined.
The optional chaining on mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration is redundant since you already check mainHostDestinationCalendar in the ternary condition.

Logic error: when externalCalendarId is provided, you're searching for a calendar where externalId === externalCalendarId, but this will always fail since you're looking for a calendar that matches itself. Should likely find by credentialId or use different logic.

Logic inversion in organization creation: The slug property is now conditionally set when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true, instead of when it's false as originally intended. This change, combined with requestedSlug still being set when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true, results in both properties being set when billing is enabled, and neither when disabled

The Calendar interface now requires createEvent(event, credentialId), but some implementations (e.g., Lark/Office365) still declare createEvent(event) only—this breaks the interface contract (also applies to other locations in the PR).

The `credential` may be undefined when passed to `updateEvent` if `reference.credentialId` is set but the credential is not found. This can lead to a runtime error when `updateEvent` is called with an undefined credential, which should be handled to prevent crashes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/types/Calendar.d.ts:134 — [P1, confidence 100] `destinationCalendar?: DestinationCalendar[] | null;` silently changes the webhook-facing CalendarEvent contract from an object/null to an array/null without versioning, so existing webhook consumers that read `payload.destinationCalendar.externalId` break on every newly emitted booking payload.

adjudication.rationale: The diff clearly shows the type change in packages/types/Calendar.d.ts from `destinationCalendar?: DestinationCalendar | null;` to `destinationCalendar?: DestinationCalendar[] | null;`. The webhook test file (apps/web/playwright/webhook.e2e.ts) also shows the expected value changing from `null` to `[]`, confirming this is a breaking change to the webhook payload structure. External webhook consumers that expect `payload.destinationCalendar.externalId` (object access) will break when receiving an array instead. This is a real API contract breaking change without versioning.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/features/bookings/lib/handleNewBooking.ts:1874 — [P1, confidence 100] `destinationCalendar: evt.destinationCalendar && evt.destinationCalendar.length > 0 ? { connect: { id: evt.destinationCalendar[0].id } } : undefined` persists only the first element of the new multi-host destination model, so later cancellation, reminder, reschedule, and webhook flows reload a one-element array and lose every secondary host destination; the strongest rebuttal is that booking references retain calendar IDs, but those references do not reconstruct the destinationCalendar payload consumed by those flows, so the model remains lossy.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that in handleNewBooking.ts lines 1871-1876, when creating a booking, only the first destination calendar is connected via `connect: { id: evt.destinationCalendar[0].id }`. The diff shows that `evt.destinationCalendar` is now an array (changed from single object to array throughout the codebase), and for collective team events, multiple destination calendars are pushed to this array (line 1068: `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)`). However, when persisting to the database, only the first element is saved. This means secondary host destination calendars are lost in the database, even though they were used for creating calendar events. Later flows that reload from the database will only have access to the first destination calendar, not the full array that was used during booking creation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:251 — [P1, confidence 100] `: event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId;` removes the former fallback to the event's destination calendar when a legacy booking reference has no `externalCalendarId`, so updates for those existing bookings send an undefined `calendarId` and no longer reach the calendar that originally held the event.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a logic error at line 251-253. The code `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId` is checking if externalCalendarId matches cal.externalId, but when externalCalendarId is already provided (truthy), this branch isn't reached. The issue is when externalCalendarId is falsy - the find() will search for a calendar where externalId === undefined/null, which will never match, returning undefined. The original code `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId` would have returned the first destination calendar's externalId as a fallback. This is a real bug that breaks the fallback behavior for legacy bookings.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/core/EventManager.ts:339 — [P2, confidence 75] `for (const destination of event.destinationCalendar) {` serializes one credential lookup and one remote calendar creation per collective host, making booking latency and request-timeout risk grow linearly with host count; the strongest rebuttal is that collectives are usually small, but no bound is enforced, and batching credential IDs plus parallelizing independent creates deletes the per-host query/await structure without changing behavior.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the new code at line 339 uses a sequential for-loop with await inside for creating calendar events across multiple destination calendars. Looking at the diff, the loop `for (const destination of event.destinationCalendar)` contains `await createEvent(credential, event, destination.externalId)` and potentially `await prisma.credential.findUnique()` for each destination. This is a valid performance concern - for collective events with multiple hosts, each calendar creation happens sequentially rather than in parallel. The code could use Promise.all() to parallelize these independent operations. However, this is a performance optimization concern, not a bug - the code functions correctly. The finding is grounded in actual diff code and represents a legitimate architectural concern about scalability, though the practical impact depends on typical collective team sizes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/features/bookings/lib/handleNewBooking.ts:992 — P1 confidence 75: `if (isTeamEventType && eventType.schedulingType === "COLLECTIVE" && user.destinationCalendar)` omits every collective co-host without an explicit destination-calendar row, so those hosts receive no calendar event instead of the existing primary-calendar fallback; the strongest counterargument is that only configured destinations are in scope, but a collective booking promises every selected host an event and this branch silently excludes an otherwise valid host.

adjudication.rationale: The finding misreads the code. The condition `if (isTeamEventType && eventType.schedulingType === 'COLLECTIVE' && user.destinationCalendar)` at line 992 is inside a loop that processes team members to build `teamDestinationCalendars` array. If a user doesn't have a destinationCalendar, they simply don't contribute to this array - but this doesn't mean they won't receive a calendar event. The calendar event creation happens separately through `createAllCalendarEvents` which iterates over `evt.destinationCalendar`. The organizer's calendar is always included (lines 1053-1057), and the team destination calendars are pushed to the array (line 1068). Users without explicit destination calendars would still be attendees on the event. The finding incorrectly assumes this condition controls whether hosts receive calendar events, when it only controls which destination calendars are added to the array.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that in the createAllCalendarEvents method (lines 337-385), when a credential is found (either from calendarCredentials or fetched from DB), the code creates an event and pushes it to createdEvents. However, when the credential is NOT found (credential remains undefined after both lookups), the code simply continues to the next iteration without adding any error result. This means if a host's credential was deleted, no error is recorded, and the booking could appear successful while silently dropping that host's calendar event. The code at line 369 shows `if (credential) { const createdEvent = await createEvent(...) }` with no else clause to handle the missing credential case. This is a real defect where partial failures are invisible.
